passage:
Preschool note, Holi week. Hansa, class teacher.
On Tuesday a water balloon flew over the wall and burst on our window. Jeevan was nearest. I was flustered and asked him, "Was it a big boy in a red cap?" He nodded slowly. By lunchtime he was telling everyone about "the red-cap boy". Today, describing it to his mother, he added a feather to the cap.
Our guard, who saw the whole thing, says it was two girls from the lane, no caps at all. My question put the cap there.
From now on I will ask children only "What did you see?" and write down their first words.

qa.q: What burst on the window?
qa.a: A water balloon.

qa.q: How does Jeevan seem to feel about the red-cap boy now?
qa.a: He seems sure and excited about the memory, not knowing the cap came from the teacher's question.

qa.q: What will Hansa do differently, and why?
qa.a: Ask only "What did you see?" and note the first words, so questions don't plant details.

qa.q: What might Jeevan's mother think on hearing about the feather?
qa.a: She may believe the vivid detail, not knowing the teacher's question had seeded it.

grounding: A teacher's festival-week note shows a leading question planting a red cap in a young child's memory that grows more detailed with each retelling.

During the monsoon, a goat went missing from the courtyard of Bidisha's village house. Her little niece Rajni had been playing on the verandah. Bidisha knelt beside her, worried. "Rajni, did you see a tall man with a big stick take her?" Rajni thought, then nodded.
That evening she told her grandmother, "A tall man with a stick took our goat!" By the next morning the man had a black umbrella too.
Then the goat walked back from the neighbour's field, mud up to her knees, all alone. Bidisha looked at Rajni, puzzled, then thought back. She had said "tall man" and "stick" first.

qa.q: Where did the goat come back from?
qa.a: From the neighbour's field.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel telling her grandmother about the tall man?
qa.a: She felt sure and a little excited, believing she really remembered him.

qa.q: What could Bidisha have asked instead?
qa.a: An open question like "What did you see?", letting Rajni use her own words.

qa.q: What might Bidisha feel realising she said "tall man" first?
qa.a: She likely feels surprised and a bit guilty, seeing that her worried question created the memory.

grounding: Shows an adult's worried, leading question during the monsoon planting a man with a stick in a young child's memory.

passage:
On a snowy January afternoon in Montreal, Ines came home from kindergarten with only one red mitten. Her mother, Leila, sighed. "Did the man with the beard on the bus pick it up?" Ines thought hard. "Yes. He had a big beard."
At dinner she told her father the bearded man had put her mitten in his bag. By bedtime he also had a blue hat.
The next morning Leila found the missing mitten stuffed inside Ines's own coat sleeve. Ines frowned. "But I saw the beard man." Leila hugged her, wondering where that beard had come from, until she remembered her own question.

qa.q: Where was the missing mitten found?
qa.a: Stuffed inside Ines's own coat sleeve.

qa.q: Why did Ines frown when the mitten turned up?
qa.a: She felt confused, because the bearded man felt like a real memory to her.

qa.q: What could Leila ask next time something goes missing?
qa.a: An open question like "What happened on the bus?", without suggesting who took it.

qa.q: What might Leila feel when she remembers her own question?
qa.a: She may feel sheepish and surprised that her guess had become Ines's memory.

grounding: Shows a parent's leading question in winter planting a bearded man in a young child's memory, who then adds more false details.

passage:
Class note, Grade 5 writing week. Parul, class teacher.
Nikita wrote a lovely piece about her family's trip to Goa "when I was four": the crab that bit Papa's toe, the waiter who dropped the ice cream, the rain on the last day. When I asked which part she remembered best, she hesitated. "The crab. I think. Or maybe Didi has told it so many times that I just see it." Her family tells the crab story every Diwali. She couldn't say which parts she saw herself and which she had been told, and she seemed a bit unsettled by that.
Next week I'll ask the class to star the bits they remember themselves, and we'll talk about how memories mix.

qa.q: What bit Papa's toe?
qa.a: The crab.

qa.q: How did Nikita seem to feel when she couldn't separate the memories?
qa.a: She seemed a bit unsettled and uncertain, surprised she couldn't tell seeing from being told.

qa.q: Why is starring the remembered bits a useful exercise?
qa.a: It helps children notice which parts are their own memory and which come from family retellings.

qa.q: How might Didi feel knowing her retellings shaped Nikita's memory?
qa.a: Didi might be amused or touched that her story became part of Nikita's own picture of the trip.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child's memory of a family trip blending with years of family retelling until she cannot tell what she saw from what she heard.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today at lunch we talked about the trip to Nani's village when I was five. Ritu didi said I fell into the pond and Mummy pulled me out by my frock. Everyone laughed. I laughed too. I can SEE it: the green water, my pink frock, Mummy's wet sari.
But then Mummy said it was actually Ritu didi's little brother who fell in, and I only cried because he did. Ritu didi said, "No, it was Seema!" Now I don't know. The picture in my head is so clear. Was I in the pond or on the edge?
I think I've heard the story so many times it moved into my own memory. That's weird.
Seema

qa.a: Pink.

qa.a: Seema feels confused and a bit uneasy, unsure whether the memory is real or borrowed from retellings.

grounding: A child's diary shows a memory of a family trip mixing with what relatives have said since, until the child cannot tell what really happened.

passage:
Every winter evening by the chulha, Samir told the story of the Pushkar fair: how the camel knelt, how Tanvir climbed up in his red sweater, how the camel stood and Tanvir screamed. Tanvir was eight when he started telling it himself, adding the camel's bell and the man selling hot jalebis. At school he wrote it up as "My Best Day".
Then Ammi found the old photo: Samir on the camel, in the red sweater, and little Tanvir on Abbu's shoulders, crying. "You never rode it, beta. You were too scared."
Tanvir stared at the photo. He could still feel the camel rising under him. "But I remember it," he said quietly.

qa.q: Who was wearing the red sweater in the photo?
qa.a: Samir, on the camel.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he said "But I remember it"?
qa.a: He felt confused and a little sad, because the retold memory felt completely real.

qa.a: Samir might laugh or feel surprised, realising his retellings had given Tanvir the ride.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage:
Ritu, you're so sure the bus hit that cyclist first? Let your Vijay chacha tell you something. At twenty, I saw a small accident outside my college in Kanpur: a scooter clipped a rickshaw, nobody badly hurt. That evening the local paper said a speeding tempo had caused it. My friends in the hostel all repeated that.
By the next week, when the traffic constable asked me, I described the tempo: blue, loud, fast. I was completely certain. Then the rickshaw-wallah's son showed the constable a video from a shop camera. No tempo at all. Just the scooter and a pothole. I had borrowed the tempo from the paper and felt sure it was mine.
So, beta: what did you see yourself?

qa.q: What did the shop camera video show?
qa.a: No tempo at all; just the scooter and a pothole.

qa.q: How did young Vijay feel describing the tempo to the constable?
qa.a: Young Vijay felt completely certain and confident, not realising the tempo came from the paper.

qa.a: Writing down what Vijay saw that same day, before reading the paper or hearing friends.

qa.q: How might the rickshaw-wallah's son have felt when the video settled it?
qa.a: The son likely felt relieved that the truth was clear and nobody was wrongly blamed.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage:
It was raining hard in the Dadar vegetable market when Aparna saw a handcart tip over and a delivery bike skid. It lasted two seconds; for one of them her umbrella was over her eyes. By night the local group chat had fifty messages: "bike was going too fast", "rider was on his phone", "red helmet".
Next morning Aparna told her friend Gopika the whole story: the rider on his phone, the red helmet, the speed.
"You saw his phone? In that rain?" Gopika asked.
"Yes, clearly," Aparna said. Then she paused. Did she? She remembered the umbrella and the crash of cabbages. The phone and the helmet had arrived later, from the messages. It didn't feel that way. It felt like seeing.

qa.q: What tipped over in the market?
qa.a: A handcart.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when she paused?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and doubtful, realising her confident details might have come from the chat.

qa.q: What could Aparna do before repeating the story again?
qa.a: Separate what she saw from what she read, and say she isn't sure about the phone and helmet.

qa.q: What would change if Gopika hadn't asked her question?
qa.a: Aparna would likely keep telling the borrowed details as fact, and others might believe them.

grounding: Shows a young adult who witnessed a brief accident adding details from chat messages and feeling certain of them, though confidence is not proof.

Aadhya saw the auto brush a cyclist outside the college gate in Pune while she was buying chai; it took a blink. The cyclist got up, dusted himself off and rode away.
That night a local news page posted: "Speeding auto hits student near college, driver flees." The class group shared it forty times. By Friday, when the principal asked for witnesses, Aadhya told him the auto was speeding and the driver had sped off without looking back. She felt completely sure.
Afterwards her friend Arohi said, "I thought you said the cyclist just rode away?" Aadhya opened her mouth. She had said that, on Monday. When had the fleeing driver arrived in her memory?

passage:
I'm Pallavi, and in my second year of teaching I learned to shut my own mouth. A flower vase fell off the reading-corner shelf during lunch, and Damini was the only child nearby. My first instinct was to ask whether one of the rough boys had pushed it. I stopped myself. Instead I knelt and said, "Tell me what happened."
Damini said the fan blew the curtain, and the curtain knocked the vase. I wrote it down right away in my diary, with the time, before anyone else could talk to her. By home time other children had theories, and by the next day Damini was half-repeating them. But I had her first words on paper: the curtain and the fan.
The fan is now set lower.

qa.q: What did Damini say knocked the vase?
qa.a: The curtain; the fan blew the curtain.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when tempted to ask about the rough boys?
qa.a: Pallavi felt a quick pull of suspicion, then caution, not wanting to plant an idea in Damini's memory.

qa.q: Why did writing it down right away matter?
qa.a: Damini's first account was saved before other children's theories could reshape it.

qa.q: How might Damini feel being asked "Tell me what happened"?
qa.a: Damini may feel calm and trusted, free to describe what she saw without being steered.

grounding: A young teacher describes asking a child an open question instead of suggesting a culprit, and recording the account at once before it could be reshaped.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Ayesha, school counsellor.
A parent's car was scratched in the school car park this morning, and Lalit, from Class 4, was said to have seen it. Two teachers had already started asking him, "It was the Class 8 boys on cycles, right?" I asked to speak to him alone first.
I said, "Tell me what you saw, from the start." He described a white van reversing, then stopping. No cycles. I wrote down his words exactly, with the time, and read them back to him. He nodded. Later, when others asked him again, he began adding cycles, "maybe".
I have shared my first note with the principal and asked staff to use open questions only.

qa.q: What did Lalit describe reversing?
qa.a: A white van.

qa.q: What might Ayesha have been worried about when asking to speak to Lalit alone?
qa.a: Ayesha was likely worried that the teachers' leading question about cycles would change Lalit's memory.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that protected Lalit's account?
qa.a: Asked an open question, wrote down Lalit's exact words with the time, and read them back.

qa.q: How might the Class 8 boys have been affected if the leading question had won?
qa.a: They could have been wrongly blamed for a scratch caused by a van.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows an adult gathering a child's account with an open question and recording it at once, before leading questions reshape it.

passage:
Saturday night.
At the birthday party a gift went missing from the table, and my niece Chandrika had been sitting right there. Two aunties started asking her, "Was it the boy in the blue shirt? He was near the table, na?" I saw her face going blank, ready to agree.
So I took her to the balcony and asked, "What happened near the gift table?" She said a lady in a yellow dupatta moved the presents to the bedroom to make space. Nothing about a boy. I typed her exact words into my phone right then, with the time.
Later we found the gift on the bed. If I'd let the blue-shirt question stand, I think she'd have "remembered" him by tomorrow.
Zainab

qa.q: Where was the missing gift found?
qa.a: On the bed.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling watching Chandrika's face go blank?
qa.a: Zainab felt worried that Chandrika was about to agree with the aunties rather than tell her own memory.

qa.a: Took her aside, asked an open question, and typed her exact words right away with the time.

qa.q: How might the boy in the blue shirt have been affected?
qa.a: He could have been wrongly blamed and embarrassed if Chandrika had agreed with the aunties.

At the panchayat meeting in their village near Nashik, Kishore stood up, red in the face. "Urmila tai's family moved the boundary stone last monsoon! I remember it was near the mango tree."
Urmila had her own memory: the stone had always been by the well. She felt her anger rise, then made herself say, "This is how I remember it, but memory can be wrong. Let's look for something real."
She thought of her cousin's wedding photos from three years ago, taken in that field. On her phone, there it was: the stone, by the well, with the bride's red sari beside it. Kishore stared at the screen, then sat down slowly. "Maybe I mixed it up with another field."

In their London flat, Kofi held up the burnt pan. "You left the hob on, Layla. I remember you cooking eggs last night."
Layla's first instinct was to snap back; she was sure she had made toast. Instead she said, "This is how I remember it: toast, no hob. But I've been wrong before. Can we check?"
Kofi rolled his eyes but nodded. Layla scrolled her phone and found the photo she'd sent her sister at 8 p.m.: toast, jam, the cold hob in the corner. Then Kofi remembered: his friend had made noodles at eleven. He winced. "Sorry. I was so sure."
"Me too, about lots of things," Layla said. "That's why I like photos."

qa.q: What did Layla's photo show?
qa.a: Toast, jam, the cold hob in the corner.

qa.q: What did Layla feel when Kofi blamed her?
qa.a: She felt a flash of irritation and certainty, but chose to hold her memory lightly.

qa.a: She said how she remembered it, admitted she could be wrong, and looked for a photo instead of arguing.

qa.q: How did Kofi feel when he remembered his friend's noodles?
qa.a: He felt sheepish and sorry, having been just as sure and wrong.

grounding: Shows an adult in a flat-share dispute saying 'this is how I remember it' and checking a photo, since confident memory can still be wrong.

The cyclone warning flashed on every news channel in Chennai: stay indoors, move vehicles to higher ground, keep supplies ready. Gopika lay on the sofa scrolling. "Amma, they say this every year. Nothing ever happens on our street."
Her mother, Bhavna, was already filling water bottles. "Last year was nothing. This one is different."
Gopika shrugged and went back to her videos. She had lived here all her life. The worst so far had been a wet school shoe.
By evening the wind was howling and water was creeping up the ground-floor steps. Bhavna called the building secretary, moved the family documents and Paati's medicines upstairs, and made Gopika carry the torch and the phone charger.

qa.q: What had been the worst so far for Gopika?
qa.a: A wet school shoe.

qa.q: Why did Gopika feel so calm about the warning?
qa.a: She felt safe and unbothered because nothing bad had ever happened on her street, so the warning felt unreal.

qa.q: What could Gopika do next time a warning comes?
qa.a: Take official warnings seriously, help pack essentials early, and not rely on the past to predict what will happen.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt as Gopika kept scrolling?
qa.a: She was likely worried and frustrated, preparing alone while her daughter shrugged.

grounding: Shows a teenager shrugging off a cyclone warning and scrolling on because nothing bad has happened before, while a parent takes protective steps.

passage:
Looking back, I'm amazed how calm I was. I'm Tenzin, and last monsoon the district sent a landslide alert for our hillside in Sikkim. The hostel warden, Naveen sir, told us to pack a bag and be ready to move to the school hall. I didn't pack. I lay on my bunk scrolling, thinking: I've lived on this hill for sixteen years. The hill doesn't move.
At midnight a crack of stones woke us, and Naveen sir was calling names in the corridor with a torch. I went down in slippers, no bag. In the morning we saw a slide had covered the path behind the hostel. Nobody was hurt. But I still think about how normal everything felt, right up to the sound.

qa.q: Where were the students told to move?
qa.a: To the school hall.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while lying on the bunk?
qa.a: Tenzin felt calm and safe, sure the hill wouldn't move because it never had.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do differently at the next alert?
qa.a: Pack the bag at once and follow the warden's instructions, rather than trusting that ordinary days will continue.

qa.q: What might Naveen sir have felt at midnight?
qa.a: Naveen sir was likely frightened and focused, rushing to account for every student with a torch.

grounding: A teenager looks back on ignoring a landslide alert because the hillside had always been safe, while the warden acted to protect everyone.

When the loudspeaker on the panchayat van said the river was rising fast, Vinita's family in the Kosi village didn't move at first. Her father said, "It'll stop at the field, like always." Vinita started packing properly: the steel trunk, her college certificates, the good saris, the pressure cooker. Her sister Parul kept saying, "Leave it, didi, just come." Vinita snapped at her. "I'm not losing everything because of one announcement."
Twenty minutes passed. Then water came through the door, ankle-deep, then knee-deep. They waded to the school on the high ground holding only the trunk and each other. Vinita's certificates were soaked anyway. Sitting on the school steps, she shook, angry mostly at herself.

qa.q: Where did the family wade to?
qa.a: The school on the high ground.

qa.q: Why did Vinita snap at Parul?
qa.a: She felt stressed and irritated, clinging to the usual pattern and her belongings, sure there was still time.

qa.q: What could the family do before the next monsoon?
qa.a: Keep documents in a waterproof bag ready to grab, and leave as soon as the warning comes.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt during those twenty minutes?
qa.a: Parul was likely frightened and frustrated, seeing the danger while her sister kept packing.

grounding: Shows a family under a real flood warning stopping to pack, sure it will pass like always, until the water arrives faster than expected.

The evacuation text came at 4 p.m.: wildfire approaching, residents of the valley road should leave now. Sofia, home in Greece for the summer, looked out at the hazy orange sky and decided there was time. She wanted her laptop, her grandmother's photos, the cat carrier, her good shoes.
Her neighbour Kwame knocked twice. "The road will close. Come with me."
"Ten minutes," she said.
The ten minutes became thirty. By the time she drove out, ash was falling like grey snow and police were turning cars back on the upper road. She made it down, hands shaking on the wheel, the cat yowling. Kwame was waiting at the petrol station. "I thought you'd be right behind me," he said quietly.

qa.q: What time did the evacuation text come?
qa.a: At 4 p.m.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling as she drove out through the ash?
qa.a: She felt frightened and shaken, realising how fast things had changed while she packed.

qa.q: What could Sofia prepare for the next fire season?
qa.a: A small grab bag and a short list of things to take, so she can leave the moment a warning comes.

qa.a: He was likely worried and then relieved, having expected her right behind him.

When the siren went off across the industrial estate in Ludhiana, the loudspeaker said a chemical tank two lanes away was leaking and everyone must leave by the east gate. Tanvir looked at his father. Baljeet was already unplugging the lathe. "Five minutes. These machines are our whole business."
Tanvir started packing tools into boxes too. Outside, people were running with handkerchiefs over their faces. A sharp smell crept under the shutter.
"Papa, we have to go."
"It'll pass, it always does. Remember last year's siren?"
Tanvir's eyes began to sting. He grabbed his father's arm and pulled. They left the boxes on the floor and ran for the east gate, coughing. At the medical tent, a nurse checked them both.

qa.a: He felt alarmed and urgent, finally seeing that waiting was more dangerous than losing the tools.

The fire alarm went off at 4:50, ten minutes before the quarterly report was due, and on the fourth floor of the Hyderabad office nobody stood up. Noor looked around. Madhuri was still typing. The team lead glanced at the ceiling, then back at his screen. Two interns looked at each other, then at Madhuri.
Noor felt her own hands stay on the keyboard. If it were real, surely someone would move? The alarm kept shrieking. Then Noor smelled something like burning plastic. She stood up. "I'm going down. Come on."
Madhuri blinked, as if waking, and grabbed her bag. Within a minute the whole floor was on the stairs. It turned out to be a small fire in the pantry microwave.

subtype: Colleagues stay put when the alarm rings [Observer]
passage:
In the Kochi software office, the fire alarm started during Monday's stand-up meeting. Jomon, the newest on the team, looked up. His manager, Shankar, kept talking about deadlines. The others kept nodding. Nobody's eyes left the whiteboard, but everyone's ears seemed to be on the alarm.
Jomon noticed each person sneaking a glance at Shankar, then at each other. He did it too. A minute passed.
Then the building security guard pushed open the door. "Everyone out! Stairs, not the lift!" Suddenly everyone moved at once, chairs scraping. It was a drill. But standing in the car park, Jomon kept thinking about that minute: twelve people, all waiting for one person to go first.

qa.q: Who pushed open the door?
qa.a: The building security guard.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling during that minute?
qa.a: Jomon felt uneasy and unsure, glancing at the manager and others for permission to act.

qa.q: What could Jomon do at the next alarm?
qa.a: Stand up and head for the stairs straight away, which may prompt others to follow.

qa.q: Why might Shankar have kept talking?
qa.a: He may have assumed it was a false alarm or wanted to seem calm, not realising everyone was waiting on him.

grounding: Shows a new employee noticing that nobody reacts to a fire alarm because each person looks to the others, until someone makes the first move.

subtype: Colleagues stay put when the alarm rings [Observer]
passage:
"Francis, is that the fire alarm?"
"Probably a test. They never tell us."
"Nobody's moving."
"Exactly. If it was real, someone would go."
"Everyone's thinking that. Look, the accounts team is doing the same thing, looking at us."
"So?"
"So everyone's waiting for everyone."
"Irfan, sit down, you'll look silly."
"I'd rather look silly." Irfan stood and raised his voice. "I'm going down. Anyone coming?"
Chairs scraped. The accounts team stood up almost at once, as if they had been waiting for permission.
On the stairs, Francis muttered, "Okay. That was fast."
"They were all ready to go," Irfan said. "Nobody wanted to be first."

qa.q: What did Francis think the alarm probably was?
qa.a: A test.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when told he'd look silly?
qa.a: Irfan felt a moment of embarrassment but more concern, choosing safety over looking silly.

qa.q: Why did Irfan's action work so quickly?
qa.a: Everyone was waiting for a cue; one person moving gave the others permission to go.

qa.q: How might the accounts team have felt when Irfan stood up?
qa.a: They likely felt relieved, having been ready to go but unwilling to be first.

grounding: Shows an employee seeing coworkers stay put through a fire alarm, each watching the others, until one person moves and the rest follow.

passage:
At the three-day training at the convention centre in Pune, Omkar did what he always did on the first morning: he walked the corridor and counted doors to the nearest exit. Four doors, then the green sign. His colleague Vaibhav laughed. "Planning an escape from the lecture?"
On day two, halfway through a session, the alarm sounded. The speaker paused. People looked at each other. Omkar picked up his bag, which held his phone, a torch and a small first-aid pouch, and walked out, counting doors. A few people followed.
On the lawn, the organisers announced a faulty sensor. Vaibhav grinned. "All that for nothing." Omkar shrugged. "I'd rather be embarrassed on a lawn than late on the stairs."

qa.q: What was in Omkar's bag?
qa.a: His phone, a torch and a small first-aid pouch.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Vaibhav teased him on the lawn?
qa.a: Omkar seemed calm and unbothered, preferring a little embarrassment to being late in a real emergency.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's habits would help in a real fire?
qa.a: Knowing the exit route in advance and leaving at once with a small kit, without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see these habits after a real emergency?
qa.a: He might feel grateful and see them as sensible rather than funny.

grounding: Shows an adult who notes exits, carries a small kit and leaves at the first alarm, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.

passage:
Dear Hemant,
Since you've just moved to Vizag, here's what I learned in my first cyclone season. When the official warning came in October, most of my neighbours said, "Let's see if it actually hits." I didn't wait. I already had a small kit by the door: torch, power bank, water, dry snacks, copies of documents in a zip bag, my medicines. I had checked the route to the community hall.
When the district told our street to move, I went that afternoon. The cyclone turned north; our street got only rain. Some people teased me for running away. I felt a bit silly, honestly. But silly and safe is a good trade.
Please make your kit this weekend.
Love, Lavanya

qa.q: In which month did the official warning come?
qa.a: In October.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about being teased by the neighbours?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a bit silly but still sure that being safe was worth it.

qa.q: What should Hemant do this weekend?
qa.a: Make a small kit like Lavanya's and learn the routes to safe places near the new home.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who waited have felt when the cyclone turned?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved and confident, perhaps not noticing how lucky they had been.

grounding: A young adult's letter describes keeping a small kit, knowing routes and following an official warning early, preferring embarrassment to being late.

passage:
Divyansh, you asked about my gas leak story for the podcast. Sure. I'm Ankita, and I'm the person who leaves first. One night last winter I smelled gas in our building corridor. Faint, but there. My neighbours said, "It's always a bit smelly, it's the old pipes." I didn't argue.
I opened the windows, didn't touch any switches, knocked on two doors, went downstairs and called the gas company's emergency line, like the sticker by the meter says. Then I waited outside in my pyjamas for forty minutes. They found a small loose joint and fixed it. Nothing dramatic.
Everyone came down to see why I was out in the cold in pyjamas. I was embarrassed. But I'd do it again tomorrow.

qa.q: How long did Ankita wait outside?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel standing outside in pyjamas?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed in front of the neighbours, yet sure the choice was right.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's steps followed the official advice?
qa.a: Calling the gas company's emergency line, as the sticker by the meter says, after opening windows and avoiding switches.

qa.q: How might the neighbours see Ankita now?
qa.a: They might see Ankita as over-careful, or feel grateful once they learn about the loose joint.

grounding: A young adult describes acting on a faint gas smell at once and following the official instructions, preferring mild embarrassment to waiting for proof.

passage:
Dear diary,
Disaster. I swallowed my gum in PT. Dilnaz screamed, "Now it'll stay in your stomach for SEVEN YEARS!" Everyone knows that. My cousin says it, the bus boys say it, even Dilnaz's big sister. I've heard it about a hundred times, so it must be true.
I kept touching my tummy all through maths.
At home I told Mummy, almost crying. She laughed a little, then hugged me and said it just passes through like food, and if my tummy ever hurts I should tell her. She said lots of things people repeat aren't true; they only sound true because we've heard them so often.
I still feel weird. But Mummy doesn't lie.
Preeti

qa.q: Where did Preeti swallow the gum?
qa.a: In PT.

qa.q: Why was Preeti so sure the gum would stay for seven years?
qa.a: Preeti felt scared and certain, because hearing it so many times made it feel true.

qa.q: What could Preeti ask the next time a playground fact is scary?
qa.a: Where it comes from, and whether someone who really knows, like Mummy or a teacher, agrees.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel if she learned the fact was wrong?
qa.a: Dilnaz might feel surprised and a bit sheepish, having shouted it so confidently.

grounding: A child's diary shows believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it, as familiarity makes it feel true.

passage:
In Harsha's village, every child knew that if you swallowed a watermelon seed, a plant would grow in your stomach. The older boys said it at the pond, the girls said it at the handpump, and even the bangle-seller joked about it at the fair.
So when Harsha swallowed a seed at his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays, he went pale. "It'll grow out of my mouth," he whispered.
Payal, who was in Class 8 and read everything, laughed. "It doesn't work like that. Seeds need soil and light."
Harsha didn't believe her. Everybody had said it, so many times. For three days he checked his tongue in the mirror every morning.

qa.q: Where did Harsha swallow the seed?
qa.a: At his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays.

qa.q: Why didn't Harsha believe Payal?
qa.a: He felt frightened, and the 'fact' felt truer because he had heard it from everyone so many times.

qa.q: What could help Harsha trust the real explanation?
qa.a: Checking with a teacher or a book, and noticing that hearing something often doesn't make it true.

qa.q: How might Payal feel watching Harsha check his tongue?
qa.a: Payal might feel amused but also a little sorry for how scared he is.

grounding: Shows a village child believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it, so it feels truer than a correct explanation.

passage:
At her school in Madrid, Yuki heard it in her first week: the last toilet on the second floor was haunted, and if you knocked three times, a cold hand touched your shoulder. Pablo said it. Then Lucia. Then the twins. By the end of the month Yuki had heard it maybe twenty times, and it felt as true as her own address. She walked all the way down to the ground-floor toilet, even in the rain.
When the teacher asked the class who had actually felt the hand, nobody raised theirs. "But everyone says it," Yuki said. Pablo shrugged. "My brother told me."
Yuki still took the stairs down. Knowing nobody had felt it didn't stop it feeling true.

qa.q: Which toilet was said to be haunted?
qa.a: The last toilet on the second floor.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she still took the stairs down?
qa.a: She still felt uneasy and scared, because the story felt familiar and so felt true.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to help the class?
qa.a: Talk about how hearing something often makes it feel true, and perhaps visit the toilet together to show it's ordinary.

qa.q: How does Pablo seem to feel about the story now?
qa.a: Pablo seems unbothered, shrugging and passing it off on his brother.

grounding: Shows a child believing a ghost story because classmates repeat it so often that its familiarity makes it feel true.
